questions.title: How does the Federal Circuit define 'substantial evidence' in the context of TTAB factual findings, and how does this differ from the 'de novo' review applied to legal conclusions?
questions.question_body: In *Apex Bank v. CC Serve Corp.*, the court states it reviews the Board's legal conclusions de novo but its findings of fact for substantial evidence. I understand 'de novo' means looking at the issue fresh, but I'm struggling with the 'substantial evidence' standard. Does this mean I just have to find *any* piece of evidence in the record that supports the Board, even if I think another interpretation is better? Or do I have to look at the whole record to see if a reasonable mind could accept it? How exactly does this standard limit my ability to overturn a factual finding like the similarity of services?

questions.title: Can a trademark registrant claim ownership over a generic term like 'ASPIRE' if they are merely an intermediary service provider rather than a direct issuer of financial products?
questions.question_body: CC Serve owns the ASPIRE mark for credit card services, but they don't actually issue the cards; they partner with banks who do. Apex argued that since CC Serve isn't providing traditional banking services (like deposits or loans), their services aren't identical to Apex's planned 'banking and financing' services. However, the Board found them 'legally identical, in part.' If a company acts as an administrator or processor for credit cards rather than a lender, can they still assert rights against a new bank entering the market under a similar name? Doesn't this stretch the definition of 'services' too far?

questions.title: Is there a requirement for consistency in defining 'similar goods/services' across different DuPont factors within the same proceeding?
questions.question_body: This is where I'm most confused about the court's reasoning. The Board found in Factor 2 that Apex's banking services and CC Serve's credit card services were highly similar (even partially identical). Yet, when moving to Factor 6 (third-party marks), the Board suddenly narrowed its scope *only* to marks used strictly for 'credit card services,' excluding broader banking/financing marks. The Federal Circuit called this an error. Why is it legally required that if Factor 2 says 'these industries overlap,' Factor 6 must use that same broad definition of overlap? Can't one argue that while banking and credit cards are related generally (Factor 2), third-party competition is only fierce specifically within credit card administration (Factor 6)?

questions.title: What constitutes sufficient proof of 'commercial weakness' under DuPont Factor 6, and why did nine third-party uses fail to meet that threshold?
questions.question_body: Apex submitted evidence showing nine other uses of 'Aspire' or Aspire-formative marks in credit card services. The Board dismissed this, saying nine wasn't enough to prove 'considerable' or 'ubiquitous' use needed to weaken CC Serve's mark. They cited cases mentioning 14 or 26 examples as significant. Is there a hard numerical rule here? Or is it purely qualitative? If nine companies are using similar names in a crowded financial sector, shouldn't that logically make consumers more sophisticated at distinguishing sources? Why didn't nine suffice here?

questions.title: Why did the Federal Circuit vacate the analysis of DuPont Factor 1 (Similarity of Marks) based entirely on errors made in Factor 6?
questions.question_body: The court affirmed Factor 2 but vacated Factors 1 and 6. My understanding is that Factor 1 looks at visual/sound/conceptual similarity ('ASPIRE BANK' vs. 'ASPIRE'). Usually, this seems like an independent inquiry based on how words look and sound. However, the court said they had to vacate Factor 1 because reconsidering Factor 6 might change the determination of 'commercial strength,' which affects commercial impression. Isn't commercial impression mostly about how consumers perceive two specific side-by-side marks regardless of how many other people use similar words elsewhere? How does third-party usage legally alter the inherent similarity between two specific marks?

questions.title: Does an Intent-to-Use application grant priority rights superior to existing registrations during an opposition proceeding before actual use begins?
questions.question_body: Apex filed an Intent-to-Use (ITU) application in August 2019 with a priority date tied to filing, while CC Serve had registered ASPIRE back in 1998 with a priority date of 1996. Since Apex hadn't launched their internet bank yet at the time of opposition, did they have any standing to argue their mark was valid against CC Serve's long-standing registration? How does ITU status interact with Section 2(d) oppositions when there is no actual commerce yet?
